topics.title: loop gain
topics.essence: Break the feedback loop, inject a signal and see what comes back around: the loop gain T. Feedback divides errors, distortion and gain drift by 1 + T, so its benefits last only at frequencies where |T| is large.
topics.check: An op-amp with open-loop gain 10⁴ is wired as a non-inverting amplifier that feeds back a tenth of the output. What is T, and how much does a 10% drop in open-loop gain change the closed-loop gain?

topics.title: gain-bandwidth trade
topics.essence: Wrap feedback round a single-pole amplifier and the gain falls by 1 + T while the bandwidth rises by 1 + T. Their product stays at the unity-gain frequency, so every decade of closed-loop gain costs a decade of bandwidth.
topics.check: An op-amp's gain falls to 1 at 10 MHz. You build a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 100. What bandwidth do you expect, and what happens if you lower the gain to 10?

topics.title: phase margin
topics.essence: Negative feedback turns positive if the loop delays the signal by 180° while |T| is still 1 or more. Phase margin is how far the loop's phase is from −180° where |T| = 1. A small margin means ringing; none means oscillation.
topics.check: A loop gain has one pole far below crossover and a second pole exactly at the frequency where |T| = 1. What is the phase margin, and what does the closed-loop step response look like?

links.why: G/(1 + GH) approaches 1/H only when the product GH, the loop gain, is large.
The loop gain is the product of every block met going once around the loop.
With one dominant pole the open-loop gain falls as 1/ω, so gain times bandwidth is constant.
The same 1 + T divides the gain and multiplies the bandwidth.
Read the frequency where |T| crosses 0 dB, then read the phase there.
Stability is a property of the loop gain T, not of the forward gain alone.
A closed-loop pole crosses into the right half-plane exactly when the margin reaches zero.
